extracted.intended_audience: readers of philosophical essays; students/scholars of Montaigne; general educated public
extracted.subtask_description: A Renaissance essay (Montaigne) reflecting on human nature, comparing mankind and beasts, and weighing knowledge, ignorance, health, and virtue. The text argues by examples and aphorisms rather than by formal rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty is culturally relative
rubrics_metrics.description: We fancy the forms according to our own appetite and liking; there is no single natural rule or prescription for beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay lists cross-cultural examples (Indians paint black, Mexicans prize a low forehead, some nations blacken teeth, others stretch ears, Biscay women shave heads) to illustrate that standards of beauty vary and are shaped by custom and taste rather than universal nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Animals exhibit human-like virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: Many animals show qualities we value in humans—magnanimity, repentance, clemency, fidelity, social intelligence—often illustrated by concrete tales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided: a dog sent to Alexander that only rouses for a lion (magnanimity); an elephant that starved itself after killing its keeper (repentance); a tiger that spared a kid for two days (clemency); halcyons calming the sea during nesting; shell-fish cooperating. These are offered to challenge human exclusivity of virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism about human superiority (vanity of preferring man to other animals)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not upon any true ground of reason, but by a foolish pride and vain opinion, that we prefer ourselves before other animals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues that many animals surpass humans in various qualities (beauty, tranquillity, simplicity) and that human claims of superiority (reason, erect posture) are often poetic or vain rather than factual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obedience as the foundational virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: The first law given to man was a law of pure obedience; from obedience and submission spring all other virtues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay contrasts obedience/submission with self-opinion, which generates sin; it presents obedience as simple, not requiring disputation, and as a remedy for pride in our reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humility and submission make the complete good man
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Tis only humility and submission that can make a complete good man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text recommends prescribing duty rather than leaving it to each man's judgment, warning that unbounded individual discretion leads to the forgery of destructive duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Health is the fairest and richest present of nature (health > wisdom)
rubrics_metrics.description: Health is the most palpable good; philosophers may value wisdom, but health is a more substantial and desirable possession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay cites philosophical claims that wisdom is supreme, but argues by example (illness afflicts the learned as much as others) that health should be prized above abstract knowledge; Stoic thought and anecdotes are used to question philosophical priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge often causes anticipatory distress and suffering
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge and reasoning frequently produce in us fears, prognostics, and anxieties about future evils that ignorance would not create.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted lines: 'The plague of man is the opinion of wisdom' and examples of learned men tormented by imagined or anticipated ailments. The text argues that reasoning about future harms (prognostics) puts 'the stone in his soul before he has it in his bladder.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure defined chiefly as absence of pain (Epicurean viewpoint)
rubrics_metrics.description: That school fixes the greatest pleasure chiefly in unconsciousness of pain; to be freed from ill is the greatest good a man can hope for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay draws on Epicurean phrasing (e.g., 'Nimium boni est, cui nihil est mali') to express that many pleasures aim ultimately at attaining insensibility to pain; the active 'itching' pleasures still have the mark of relieving torment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophy does not immunize one from bodily suffering
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning or philosophical attainment does not exempt a man from pain, sickness, shame, or other human inconveniences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anecdotes (Posidonius, Arcesilas, Dionysius Heracleotes) show philosophers in pain who fail to live up to their stoical professions; the essay uses these to argue that knowledge seldom yields practical protection against physical afflictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: True endurance arises from habituation, not theoretical knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Endurance and steadiness in the face of suffering are more commonly found in those bred to hardship (gladiators, muleteers) than in theoreticians or philosophers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay contrasts abstract philosophical precepts with the real-world toughness of people accustomed to harsh conditions, concluding that practice and habituation produce genuine fortitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and ignorance conduce to serenity and longevity
rubrics_metrics.description: A simple, ignorant life (without letters, law, kings, or religion) tends to produce a serene soul and long life, free from the anxieties of learned forecasting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author attributes the reputed longevity and easy deaths of some peoples to the tranquillity of their minds rather than solely to climate; simplicity of soul is emphasised as protective of well-being.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reason's predictive imagination can be more harmful than helpful
rubrics_metrics.description: The quick motion, penetration, and subtlety we call reason are pestiferous to many and salutary to few, because they generate anticipation of evils and unnecessary preoccupation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay recommends caution in overvaluing reason's prognostic habits: it can make us imagine sickness and disaster that have not yet occurred, diminishing present wellbeing and prompting needless precautions or treatments.

rubrics_metrics.name: The opinion of wisdom (pride) corrupts proper religious acknowledgment
rubrics_metrics.description: So long as man believes he has means and power of himself, he will never acknowledge what he owes to his Maker; pride in wisdom is an impediment to gratitude and obedience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text connects philosophical pride—e.g., claiming equality with godlike virtue—to a failure to submit and be humble, urging that such vanity be repudiated to restore proper relation to the divine and to virtue.
